title: Trust without contracts
bodyMd:
In the market square of a mid-sized town, a few dozen traders sell cheese, vegetables and cured meats every Saturday. Almost none of their dealings with customers are written down. A buyer who finds that a wheel of cheese is spoiled inside has no receipt, no warranty and, in practice, no court to turn to, since the sums involved are too small to be worth a lawsuit. Yet complaints are rare, and traders routinely replace faulty goods without argument.

The explanation most often offered is that market people are simply more honest than others. A more modest explanation does better. A trader who returns to the same pitch every week is playing a long game. Cheating a customer might gain a few euros today, but that customer will not come back, and in a square where shoppers talk to one another, others may not come either. The value of a good name is the stream of future sales it protects, and that stream is worth far more than any single deception. Honesty, on this account, is not the cause of the market's good behaviour so much as its product.

The account also predicts where the arrangement should fail. A stall that appears for a single summer fair, selling to strangers who will never see it again, has little future to protect, and buyers at such fairs are accordingly warier. The same logic suggests why the Saturday traders treat newcomers to the town with particular care: a first purchase is the moment at which a reputation is either founded or lost.

It would be wrong to conclude that formal rules are unnecessary. Reputation works only as fast as news travels, and only among people who meet repeatedly. It is a poor guard against a seller about to retire, or against one whose customers are too scattered to compare notes. Where those conditions hold, contracts and courts do work that a good name cannot. The square shows not that law is redundant, but that much of what holds a market together is unwritten.
accessibilityText: A four-paragraph prose passage of about 340 words on reputation in a hypothetical weekly town market. The first paragraph describes traders whose dealings are not written down; a buyer with spoiled goods has no receipt or warranty, and the sums are too small for a lawsuit, yet complaints are rare and faulty goods are replaced. The second paragraph rejects the view that market people are simply more honest and argues instead that a trader returning each week protects a stream of future sales by behaving well, so that honesty is less the cause of the good behaviour than its product. The third paragraph says the account predicts failure at a one-off summer fair, where buyers are warier, and explains why traders take particular care with newcomers. The fourth paragraph warns that formal rules are still needed where news travels slowly, where people do not meet repeatedly, with a seller about to retire, or with scattered customers, and concludes that much of what holds a market together is unwritten.

provenance.notes: Original expository prose written for this question bank. The market and town are invented for illustration; no published article, essay or test passage was copied, paraphrased or reconstructed.
